description:
Found a few viburnums that were barely hanging on under some honeysuckle.  This is on a fairly steep wooded slope (2nd pic).  My approach here was to just cut the honeysuckle off at the base and allow the root system to live while the understory recovers.  I’d worry about hillside subsidence if I killed too many roots (even honeysuckle roots) too quickly.  Third pic shows a fairly intact herbaceous layer.  Trout lily, purple cress, water leaf, toad-shade, and larkspur all exist in numbers so don’t want the hillside to erode too quickly.  

The second pic shows the honeysuckle piles in a small ditch below the hillside.  I drove over to the west side to volunteer with Western Wildlife Corridor and this is something they did.  Pile the honeysuckle carcasses in small wooded ravines to help slow the water runoff.  I like this idea because if you leave the carcasses where they fall they make it hard to control things like garlic mustard that may sprout the year after honeysuckle removal.  This is probably part of their reasoning.

Disturbed lowland woods with a canopy of various native hardwoods, a serious invasion of Norway maple, and a typical understory composed of mostly invasive species like Privets, Burning Bush, and Multiflora Rose.

The southwest side of the loop has almost no native tree regeneration. There are some huge bitternut and shagbark hickories here, but almost every young tree growing here is a Norway maple. There are probably a couple hundred of them between 2-6" that would be great to remove at this stage. The northern section of the loop is dense with Ligustrum obtusifolium. Besides Carpinus carolinana and a few Viburnum prunifolium, a native understory is non-existent.
